digest.intro: Cryptography cracks, organs grow inside organs, and the world fragments quietly.

items.title: Thymus Transplanted Into Spleen Grows, Restores Immune Function
items.blurb: Researchers implanted donor thymic tissue into mouse spleens — not the textbook transplant site — and it grew, behaved like a real thymus (training T cells, establishing self-tolerance), and measurably improved responses to both viral infection and tumors compared to controls. The practical hook: thymic involution with age is one of the cleaner mechanistic explanations for why old immune systems fail, and the spleen turns out to be a far more hospitable host than the previously tried thigh muscle. One organ inside another, working.

items.title: The Millennium Problems, But for Biology
items.blurb: Someone has attempted to do for biology what the Clay Institute did for mathematics: enumerate the genuinely foundational unsolved problems with crisp, falsifiable criteria for what would count as a solution. The two excerpted problems alone are humbling — demonstrating abiogenesis from plausible chemistry (self-replicating cells increasing 10⁶-fold), and reversible whole-body cryopreservation of live adult mice. This is a document worth sitting with: it's a structured map of civilizational ignorance.

items.title: FDA Advisory Panel Votes to Allow BPC-157 and Mots-C Compounding
items.blurb: On July 23–24, an FDA advisory committee recommended allowing six peptides — including BPC-157 and Mots-C — to be compounded by licensed pharmacies, over objections from career scientists about thin human-trial evidence. It's a recommendation, not a finalized rule, and as this physician-authored piece is honest enough to say: neither compound is proven to treat a specific condition in humans yet. Still, it's the regulatory inflection point that determines whether these stay in gray-market vials or enter the prescription mainstream.

sections.heading: Provenance, proof, and the authentication problem

items.title: ZK-JPEG: Proving an Image Was Edited Without Revealing the Original
items.blurb: The core problem this paper solves: camera-attestation signatures (the main tool for proving an image came from a real camera) break the moment you crop, blur, or JPEG-compress the image — which you always do. ZK-JPEG builds a zero-knowledge proof that survives lossy JPEG compression, letting you prove a published image was correctly derived from an authenticated original without ever revealing that original. For anyone working at the intersection of digital and physical authenticity, this is the actual cryptographic infrastructure the provenance argument has been missing.

items.title: How to Use an LLM Without Letting It Eat Your Voice
items.blurb: The two rules are simple and hard: write everything yourself first, then feed it to the model to find flaws — and never adopt a single word it suggests, only the diagnosis. The reasoning is sharp: frontier models are supernaturally good at selecting pleasing phrases, which is exactly what makes their word choices toxic to your voice; readers detect LLM prose in parts per trillion. Using it as a copyeditor rather than a ghostwriter is structurally different from how most people use it, and the distinction actually holds up.

items.title: Defeating a Chip's Secure Boot With a Laser, One Bit at a Time
items.blurb: The Ledger Donjon security team decapsulated an RP2350 microcontroller, located the debug-enable register using photon-emission electron microscopy, then shone an infrared laser through the back of the silicon wafer at precisely the right clock cycle to flip the bits — unlocking the secure execution zone and reading out the 128-bit secret Raspberry Pi had hidden as a hacking challenge. The RP2350 has glitch detection specifically to block the usual 'zap it until it obeys' approach, so they went slower and more precise instead. Hardware security as a kind of deranged watchmaking.

facts.fact: Thymic tissue implanted into mouse spleens — not the usual site — grew normally and improved both anti-tumor and antiviral immune responses compared to controls, suggesting the spleen is a better host organ than previously tried thigh muscle.

JPEG compression invalidates camera-attestation signatures, meaning nearly every photograph shared online — even one from an authenticated camera — currently has no cryptographic proof of its provenance; ZK-JPEG is the first system to fix this while surviving lossy compression.

The FDA's compounding advisory committee voted to allow BPC-157 and Mots-C to be prepared by licensed pharmacies despite career FDA scientists objecting that human-trial evidence remains thin — and the rule is still not finalized as of this writing.

The Ledger Donjon team defeated the RP2350's secure boot — a chip specifically designed with glitch detection to resist fault injection — by firing an infrared laser through the back of the decapped silicon wafer to flip the debug-enable register bit at the right clock cycle.

art_picks.title: Daughters of the Dust
art_picks.creator: Julie Dash
art_picks.why: The first feature film by a Black woman theatrically released in the US — a non-linear, myth-saturated portrait of a Gullah family on the eve of migration. Stunning visual language built entirely on ritual, memory, and symbolic weight; the kind of film that rewires how you think about time and image. Arthur Jafa was the cinematographer.

art_picks.title: Brice Marden: Six Decades
art_picks.creator: Brice Marden
art_picks.why: The first comprehensive New York survey of Marden's paintings in twenty years — six decades of work that lives exactly at the edge between system and feeling, where grids dissolve into something almost nervous. Pure obsessive mark-making with a deep formal logic underneath.

art_picks.title: Vespertine
art_picks.creator: Björk
art_picks.why: A record built from micro-sounds — music boxes, harps, a choir of 50 voices — assembled into an impossibly intricate interior architecture. Every sound is tactile and placed. The system is the feeling. If you haven't heard it in a while, it still sounds like something that shouldn't exist.

events.name: Aziz Hazara: Coming Home
events.venue: SculptureCenter, 44-19 Purves St, Long Island City, Queens
events.why: Hazara gathered debris left at Bagram Airfield after the US military's withdrawal — kneepads, electronics, kitchenware — and returned it to exhibition as a durational act of witness; the artist himself cannot attend because his Afghan passport is currently banned from entry, which is itself part of the work.

events.name: Johanna Hedva: Gravity, My / Favorite Enemy
events.venue: Center for Art, Research and Alliances (CARA), Manhattan
events.why: Hedva works at the intersection of chronic illness, cosmology, and sound — the kind of practice that fuses body-as-system with deep-time thinking, built around feedback between pain and beauty; a genuinely unusual institutional debut for this show.

events.name: SPRING/BREAK Art Show — 'HIDE N SEEK'
events.why: The curator-driven anti-fair that takes over an unlikely raw space during Armory Week — 100+ independently curated exhibitions organized around encoded meaning, hidden symbolism, and materialist mysticism; the format is explicitly against the booth-grid model and tends to be the most formally strange thing happening that week.

events.name: Arthur Jafa: I Am Tony
events.why: The first full US survey of Jafa's nearly forty-year practice — spanning film, painting, sculpture, and photography across two floors of the newly expanded OMA-designed building — including Love is the Message, The Message is Death and new premieres; the show treats images as cultural agents with physical consequences.

events.name: The Armory Show 2026
events.venue: Javits Center, 429 11th Avenue, Hudson Yards, Manhattan
events.why: Over 230 galleries from 30 countries, with this year's focused sections on Caribbean and diasporic art — worth one pass for the sheer density of new international work, and to triangulate what the market currently thinks matters.

trial_sources.name: Contraptions — Venkatesh Rao
trial_sources.why: Rao's active post-Ribbonfarm home: long-form essays on taste cultures, technology aesthetics, coordination theory, and status — hitting at least six of the reader's core interests in a single voice.

trial_sources.name: Lifespan.io News
trial_sources.why: Independent non-profit outlet (formed by the 2024 SENS + LEAF merger) reporting daily on aging research, stem cells, rejuvenation biotech, and longevity science — credible, conflict-free, and closely matched to the reader's health and longevity track.

trial_sources.name: Kneeling Bus — Drew Austin
trial_sources.why: Recommended by Venkatesh Rao himself; Austin writes precise, unhurried essays on how technology reshapes urban behavior, social software, and the felt texture of modern life — a strong fit for the reader's interest in the aesthetics of technology and alternative institutions.
